column2: Balaam requests seven altars, seven calves and seven rams, repeating here. The three sevens remain.
Balak obeys and offers calf and ram on the altar, understood distributively across the seven from verse 1. Each is an English contextual completion.
Balak stays at the sacrifice while Balaam seeks divine encounter and promises a report. The fuller selected inquiry and straight-on clauses remain.
God appears, and Balaam reports seven prepared altars with the paired animals. The distributive each follows the stated seven.
God places the word in Balaam's mouth and commands return and speech. The message's origin remains explicit.
Balak stands with all Moabite officials beside whole burnt offerings when Balaam returns.
The selected Spirit-on-him introduction is retained before the oracle. Mesopotamia, eastern mountains and the doubled curse invitation all remain.
Two parallel questions deny a curse unsupported by the Lord/God. The different divine designations remain.
Mountain and hill views lead to the people dwelling alone and not being reckoned among nations. Them renders the collective people in natural English.
Jacob's seed and Israel's clans are counted; Balaam wishes death among righteous souls and seed like theirs. The selected seed ending is not replaced with last end.
Balak contrasts his curse commission with an emphatic actual blessing.
Balaam's question reiterates obligation to speak God's supplied word.
Another location promises only a partial view, emphatically not all, for a renewed curse attempt. The source's initial negative is retained.
The field lookout and Hewn Height summit retain the selected descriptive geography, followed by seven altars and paired animals.
Balaam again leaves Balak by the sacrifice to inquire of God; inquiry is explicit.
God meets Balaam and supplies the next word before sending him back.
Balak and all officials await beside the offering, and Balak asks what the Lord said.
Balak is commanded to rise and hear, addressed as witness and Zippor's son. The selected witness designation remains.
Led astray and threatened preserve the selected unusual predicates rather than conventional lie/repent. The two questions affirm acting and abiding by speech.
column3: The first predicate's precise lexical force needs further specialist review.

column2: Balaam is taken up to bless and will not reverse it, retaining both first-person verbs and emphatic negation.
column3: Taken up is provisional for the passive commission expression and needs a spoken-language decision.

column2: No toil or distress, divine companionship and rulers' glories remain the selected lines; no shout-of-a-king substitute is introduced.
God brings them from Egypt; the one-horned-beast glory comparison remains without assigning a modern species.
column3: The pronoun's antecedent and the elliptical comparison require fuller review.

column2: Omen-taking and divination are denied in Jacob/Israel; the timely declaration concerns what God will accomplish, retaining future reference.
The people rise as lion cub and exult as lion, then consume prey and drink slain blood before sleeping. The violent image is not softened.
Balak forbids both cursing and blessing; at all conveys the emphatic blessing prohibition.
Balaam repeats that God's spoken word determines what he does. The source says do here, not only speak.
Another site is proposed with the condition of divine pleasure, followed by another curse request.
Peor's summit extends toward the wilderness. The selected location remains provisional in conventional English form.
Seven altars, calves and rams are requested again in full.
Balak obeys with calf and ram per altar, repeating the offering pattern.
Balaam recognizes that blessing Israel is good before the Lord and ceases his customary omen-seeking, turning toward wilderness.
He sees tribal encampments; the selected Spirit comes within him, distinct from upon him in 23:7.
The oracle names Balaam and Beor and describes true seeing. No closed-eye reading is imported.
Hearing divine oracles, seeing in sleep and uncovered eyes are all retained; the vision is not recast as falling into a trance.
Jacob's houses and Israel's tents are separately praised. Human-address your remains.
Wooded valleys, river gardens, Lord-pitched tents and water-side cedars remain the four comparisons. Tents is not changed to aloes.
column3: The active shading participle's best English expression needs refinement; shaded is retained provisionally rather than claimed exact.

column2: A man emerges from the seed to rule many nations; the kingdom rises above Gog and increases. Gog is not harmonized to Agag.
God guides him from Egypt, followed by one-horned-beast glory, devoured enemy nations, marrow and missiles. The selected fat-parts image remains.
column3: The pronoun antecedents and fat-parts/marrow expression need fuller poetic and lexical review.

column2: Lion and cub rest lead to a challenge about rousing him, then reciprocal blessing and curse. The change to second-person you remains.
Balak's anger and hand-clapping accompany his complaint about the third blessing. Third links the sequence of oracles.
Balak commands flight home and attributes the lost promised honour to the Lord. His attribution remains direct speech.
Balaam appeals to what he told Balak's messengers, introducing the repeated silver-and-gold condition.
No wealth authorizes independent evil or good against the Lord's word; Balaam must speak God's speech. Evil/good is not normalized to small/great from 22:18.
Balaam announces his return and advises what this people will do to Balak's people at the end of days. The subject and object are not reversed.
The repeated oracle opening names Balaam, Beor and true seeing in full.
Hearing, knowledge from the Most High, vision in sleep and uncovered eyes all remain. The additional knowledge clause is retained.
The selected showing and blessing opening precedes star and man from Jacob/Israel, crushing Moab's rulers and plundering all Seth's sons. Man is not replaced by sceptre.
column3: Objects and pronoun relations in the two opening clauses remain provisional and need syntactic/apparatus review; no later identification of the figure is added.

column2: Edom and enemy Esau become inheritances; Israel's action is past in the selected text. Esau is not replaced by Seir.
An unnamed one arises from Jacob and destroys the city's escaping survivor. No proper identity or city-name is supplied.
Amalek begins the nations and its seed perishes. The selected seed ending remains.
The Kenite's strong dwelling and conditional rock-nest clause lead into the next verse.
Beor, a crafty nest and Assyrian captivity remain the selected difficult wording; no alternate Kenite-burning text is inserted.
column3: The relation of Beor to the nest needs apparatus and syntactic review.

column2: The selected oracle explicitly sees Og, then gives a doubled lament and question about living when God acts.
The singular emergence from the Kitians' hand shifts to plural affliction of Asshur and Hebrews, then their shared destruction. No ships are added.
column3: The implicit subjects and their referents remain unresolved for fuller discourse review.

column2: Balaam returns to his own place and Balak goes home. Both departures close the episode.
